overview.title: Choosing a tokenizer; sets vs. sequences
overview.main_topic: Practical advice on choosing a tokenizer, then the central modeling question of how to represent word order (sets vs. sequences)
overview.central_idea: For a pretrained model you must keep its tokenizer. From scratch, the compression of word or subword tokenizers is usually worth having, and subword dominates modern language models, though characters or words can suit specific needs. Representing individual tokens is easy, since they are categorical. How to represent their order is the question that separates bag-of-words (set) models, RNNs and Transformers.
overview.importance: This page links preprocessing to modeling. Its classification of architectures by how they handle order (discard it, process it step by step, or inject position information) structures sections 14.4 (set models) and 14.5 (sequence models) and leads into the Transformer in chapter 15.
learning_objectives: Explain why a pretrained model's tokenizer must be preserved
Argue why shorter inputs (from word or subword tokenization) help models track long-range dependencies
Name use cases where character-level or word-level tokenization may be preferable
Explain why tokens are categorical features and how they are encoded
Describe why word order in language is important but not canonical
Classify bag-of-words, RNN and Transformer models by how they handle order, and define 'sequence model'
prerequisites: Recurrent models from the previous chapter (timeseries)

summary:
The sidebar **"Which tokenization technique should I use?"** concludes here. With a pretrained model you must preserve its tokenization, or you **throw away the useful representations of input tokens stored in its weights**. If you build a model **from scratch**, you can tailor the tokenizer to the problem. In general, though, the **compression of word and subword tokenizers is too important to pass up**: the shorter the inputs on average, the better a model can **track long-range dependencies**, which improves performance. That is why **subword tokenization is the dominant choice for modern language models**. It handles rare or misspelled words without making common inputs longer. There is still **no one-size-fits-all** approach. **Spelling correction** might benefit from character-level tokenization, and **word-level** tokenization is simple and **interpretable**, since each input is a word a human would read, which makes ranking tokens by importance to a prediction easy. The book uses all three types in its text chapters.

**Section 14.3, Sets vs. sequences**, turns to modeling. Representing *individual tokens* is uncontroversial: they are **categorical features**, encoded as dimensions in a feature space or as category (token) vectors. The hard question is **how to encode token order**. Unlike timeseries steps, words have **no natural, canonical order**. Languages order words very differently (English vs. Japanese), the same idea can be expressed with words reshuffled, and even a fully shuffled short sentence is sometimes understandable, though often ambiguous. Order matters, but its link to meaning is not simple.

How to represent order is **the pivotal question from which NLP architectures spring**:

1. **Discard order**: treat text as an unordered set, giving **bag-of-words** models (14.4).
2. **Strict order**: process words one at a time like timeseries steps, using the **recurrent models** of the previous chapter.
3. **Hybrid**: the **Transformer** is technically order-agnostic but **injects word-position information**, so it can look at different parts of a sentence at once (unlike RNNs) while staying order-aware.

RNNs and Transformers take word order into account, so both are called **sequence models**.

paragraphs.excerpt: tokenization used during pretraining or throw out the useful representations of input tokens
paragraphs.what_it_says: Continuing from p.418: with a pretrained model you must preserve the exact tokenization used during pretraining, or throw out the useful representations of input tokens contained in the model weights.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A pretrained model's embedding rows, and everything built on them, are indexed by its tokenizer's IDs. A different tokenizer would assign different IDs and different splits, so the learned token representations would no longer correspond to the inputs.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: When you use a pretrained model the tokenizer isn't your choice; you load the one that comes with the model (e.g. RoBERTa, p.480).

terminology.meaning: A model whose weights were learned beforehand on a large corpus with a specific tokenizer.

paragraphs.excerpt: If you are building a model from scratch, you can tailor your tokenization
paragraphs.what_it_says: From scratch, you can tailor tokenization to the problem. In general the compression of word and subword tokenizers is too important to pass up: shorter average inputs let a model track long-range dependencies better and improve performance. This made subword tokenization dominant for modern language models, since it handles rare or misspelled words without making common inputs longer.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Shorter sequences put related words fewer positions apart and fit more text into a fixed context. Subword tokenization gets this compression without word-level's coverage problem: a misspelling like 'whaale' still gets encoded from pieces.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This sums up section 14.2 as a default: use subword tokenization unless there's a specific reason not to.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in attention models compute grows quadratically with sequence length, and in RNNs gradient signals weaken over many steps, so shorter sequences help both.

terminology.meaning: A relationship between tokens far apart in the sequence, e.g. a pronoun and the noun it refers to.

paragraphs.excerpt: How a machine learning model should represent individual tokens is a relatively uncontroversial
paragraphs.what_it_says: Representing individual tokens is relatively uncontroversial: they're categorical features (values from a predefined set), encoded as dimensions in a feature space or as category vectors (token vectors). The much harder question is how to encode the ordering of tokens in text.
paragraphs.what_it_means: After tokenization each token is an ID from a fixed vocabulary, a categorical variable like any other. You can one-hot it (one dimension per vocabulary entry) or map it to a dense learned vector (an embedding). Order is not something one token carries; it is a property of the whole sequence and needs its own design decision.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This moves the focus from 'what is a token' to 'how do tokens relate in sequence', which is the axis along which the chapter's models differ.

terminology.meaning: A feature taking values from a predefined set with no inherent numeric order.
A vector representing a token, either one-hot or a learned embedding.

connections: p.422: set models encode presence/absence of tokens

paragraphs.excerpt: The problem of order in natural language is an interesting one: unlike the steps
paragraphs.what_it_says: Unlike timeseries steps, words in a sentence have no natural, canonical order. Languages order similar words very differently (English vs. Japanese). Within one language the same thing can be said by reshuffling words. Even a fully randomized short sentence can sometimes be understood, though often with significant ambiguity. Order clearly matters, but its relationship to meaning isn't straightforward.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In a timeseries, position is physical time and the order is fixed. In language, order is partly grammatical convention and partly meaning ('dog bites man' vs. 'man bites dog'), and much meaning survives without it. That is why order-free models can work surprisingly well, and why order-aware models can still gain from it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It justifies trying both kinds of model: set models that ignore order (14.4) and sequence models that use it (14.5).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: English is mainly subject-verb-object, while Japanese is subject-object-verb, with particles marking grammatical roles.

terminology.meaning: A single natural ordering of elements, as time provides for a timeseries.

connections: p.427: bigram models recover some local order

paragraphs.excerpt: How to represent word order is the pivotal question from which different kinds of
paragraphs.what_it_says: How to represent word order is the pivotal question from which different NLP architectures spring. Discarding order and treating text as an unordered set gives bag-of-words models. Processing words strictly in order, one at a time like timeseries steps, uses the recurrent models of the previous chapter. As a hybrid, the Transformer is technically order-agnostic but injects word-position information, so it can look at different parts of a sentence simultaneously (unlike RNNs) while still being order-aware. RNNs and Transformers are called sequence models because they take word order into account.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The three families sit on a spectrum. Bag-of-words: order is thrown away. RNN: order is built into the computation as sequential state updates. Transformer: computation is parallel and order-free (attention treats inputs as a set), and order is added back as position information in the representations.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This taxonomy structures the rest of chapter 14 (set models, then sequence models) and chapter 15 (the Transformer).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: attention without positional information is permutation-equivariant, so shuffling the inputs just shuffles the outputs. Adding positional embeddings or encodings breaks this symmetry.

terminology.meaning: A representation of text as the set (or multiset) of its tokens, ignoring order.
A model that takes the order of input tokens into account: RNNs and Transformers.
Producing the same result, up to reordering, regardless of input order.

concepts.name: Choosing a tokenization technique
concepts.definition: Selecting character, word or subword tokenization based on whether you use a pretrained model and on the task's needs.
concepts.intuition: Pretrained: no choice. From scratch: subword by default, characters for spelling-level tasks, words for interpretability.
concepts.technical: Shorter inputs from word/subword tokenizers improve tracking of long-range dependencies.
concepts.significance: One of the first decisions in a text project, with effects on model size, speed and accuracy.
concepts.example: Spelling correction → characters; bag-of-words sentiment with interpretable weights → words; large language model → subwords.
concepts.misconception: Subword is not always optimal; the authors explicitly say there is no one-size-fits-all approach.

concepts.name: Categorical feature
concepts.definition: A feature whose values come from a predefined set without numeric meaning.
concepts.intuition: Token ID 517 isn't 'bigger' than ID 3; it is just a different category.
concepts.technical: Encoded as one-hot dimensions or as learned category vectors (embeddings).
concepts.significance: Tokens are categorical, so representing a single token is a solved problem.
concepts.example: With a 2,000-term vocabulary, a token is one of 2,000 categories → a 2,000-dim one-hot vector or a learned d-dim embedding.
concepts.misconception: Feeding raw integer IDs to a dense layer as numbers would impose a meaningless ordering.

concepts.name: Bag-of-words (set) model
concepts.definition: A model that treats text as an unordered set of tokens.
concepts.intuition: Shake the words of a review in a bag; you still know if 'terrible' is in there.
concepts.technical: Input is a multi-hot presence vector over the vocabulary; order is discarded after tokenization (p.422).
concepts.significance: Simple, fast, often strong for classification.
concepts.example: 'the movie was not good' and 'good, the movie was not' get identical representations.
concepts.misconception: Discarding order doesn't make a model useless; much meaning survives (the page's shuffled-sentence point).

concepts.name: Sequence model
concepts.definition: A model that takes the order of input tokens into account; the book names RNNs and Transformers.
concepts.intuition: It reads the sentence, not just the word list.
concepts.technical: RNNs encode order by sequential state updates; Transformers inject position information into otherwise order-agnostic attention.
concepts.significance: Needed where word order changes meaning; both families are covered in 14.5 and chapter 15.
concepts.example: Telling 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'.
concepts.misconception: The Transformer isn't inherently sequential; it is order-aware only because positional information is added.

concepts.name: Word-position information (positional encoding)
concepts.definition: Information about each token's position, added to its representation so an order-agnostic model can use order.
concepts.intuition: Stamp each word with its seat number before mixing them.
concepts.technical: The page says only that the Transformer 'injects word-position information into the representations it processes'; the mechanisms come in chapter 15.
concepts.significance: Lets Transformers be parallel (look at all positions at once) and order-aware.
concepts.example: The embedding of token 'cat' at position 2 differs from 'cat' at position 7.
concepts.misconception: Attention alone doesn't know word order.

concepts.name: Recurrent neural network (RNN)
concepts.definition: A model that processes tokens one at a time, updating a hidden state.
concepts.intuition: Reading left to right while keeping a running memory.
concepts.technical: State h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t); order is built into the computation.
concepts.significance: One of the two sequence-model families named here; from the previous chapter on timeseries.
concepts.misconception: RNNs can't look at different parts of a sentence at once; that's the advantage the page credits to Transformers.

deeper.title: Shuffled-sentence test
deeper.body: Try the page's thought experiment. 'ago years some ishmael me call' is still recognizable because the content words carry most of the meaning. 'not bad, actually good' vs. 'not good, actually bad' contain the same words but have opposite sentiment. The first case is why bag-of-words classifiers work well; the second is why sequence models can beat them. (Examples are illustrative, not from the book.)

deeper.title: Three ways to handle order
deeper.body:
| family | how order is used | parallel over positions? | where in the book |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bag-of-words / set | discarded (bigrams keep a little local order) | yes | 14.4 (pp.422-429) |
| RNN | built into sequential state updates | no | 14.5.1 (p.430) |
| Transformer | position info injected into representations | yes | chapter 15 |

deeper.title: Why shorter inputs help long-range dependencies
deeper.body: Take two related words 40 characters apart. With character tokens they are 40 positions apart; with word tokens about 8; with subwords maybe 9-10. An RNN must carry the information through every intermediate step, and each step can dilute it. An attention model must cover the whole span in its context window, with cost that grows as the window grows. Fewer positions means less dilution and a cheaper context, which is the compression argument of the sidebar. (Beyond the book.)

misconceptions.claim: You can swap in a better tokenizer when fine-tuning a pretrained model.
misconceptions.correction: You must preserve the exact pretraining tokenization; otherwise the learned token representations in the weights are thrown out.

misconceptions.claim: Subword tokenization is always the right choice.
misconceptions.correction: The authors say there is no one-size-fits-all approach: characters can help spelling correction, and words are simpler and more interpretable.

misconceptions.claim: Word order in language is like time order in a timeseries.
misconceptions.correction: The page stresses that words have no natural, canonical order; ordering varies across languages and paraphrases, and its link to meaning isn't straightforward.

misconceptions.claim: Transformers process text sequentially like RNNs.
misconceptions.correction: The Transformer is technically order-agnostic and looks at all parts of a sentence at once; it becomes order-aware only by injecting position information.

takeaways: With a pretrained model, keep its exact tokenizer, or its learned token representations are wasted.
From scratch, the compression of word/subword tokenizers usually wins, since shorter inputs help track long-range dependencies.
Subword tokenization dominates modern language models: it handles rare and misspelled words without making common inputs longer.
Characters can suit spelling correction; words are simple and interpretable.
Tokens are categorical features (one-hot or token vectors); the hard question is how to represent their order.
Bag-of-words discards order, RNNs process it step by step, and Transformers inject position info; RNNs and Transformers are sequence models.

questions.question: Why must you keep a pretrained model's tokenization?
options: Otherwise you throw out the token representations learned in the model weights
Because Keras only supports one tokenizer per model
Because pretrained models only accept characters
questions.answer: Otherwise you throw out the token representations learned in the model weights
questions.explanation: Stated in the sidebar. Speed and Keras limitations aren't the reason, and pretrained models typically use subword, not character, tokenization.

questions.question: According to the sidebar, why does shorter average input length improve performance?
questions.answer: A model can better track long-range dependencies in the text when inputs are shorter.
questions.explanation: This is the stated reason the compression offered by word and subword tokenizers is 'too important to pass up'.

questions.question: Give one task suited to character-level tokenization and one advantage of word-level tokenization, as named on this page.
questions.answer: Spelling correction may benefit from characters. Word-level is simple and interpretable, since each input is a word a human would read, which makes ranking tokens by importance to a prediction easy.
questions.explanation: Both come from the 'no one-size-fits-all' paragraph of the sidebar.

questions.question: Which statement about the Transformer matches the page?
options: It processes words strictly one at a time
It discards word order like a bag-of-words model
It is technically order-agnostic but injects word-position information
It cannot be called a sequence model
questions.answer: It is technically order-agnostic but injects word-position information
questions.explanation: The page calls it a hybrid. Strictly sequential processing describes RNNs. It doesn't discard order, because position information is added. The page explicitly calls RNNs and Transformers sequence models.

questions.question: Why is representing individual tokens called 'relatively uncontroversial'?
questions.answer: Tokens are categorical features from a predefined set (the vocabulary), and we know how to encode those, as feature-space dimensions or category (token) vectors.
questions.explanation: The difficulty lies in encoding order, not in encoding single tokens.

questions.question: How does the page argue that word order in language differs from order in a timeseries?
questions.answer: Words have no natural, canonical order: languages (English vs. Japanese) order similar words differently, the same thing can be said with reshuffled words, and even a randomized short sentence can sometimes be understood. Order matters, but its relationship to meaning isn't straightforward.
questions.explanation: Taken from the second paragraph of 14.3.

questions.question: Which models does the page call 'sequence models'?
questions.explanation: 'Because they take into account word order, both RNNs and Transformers are called sequence models.' Bag-of-words discards order.

questions.question: Can you place a bigram model on the order spectrum described here (discard / strict order / hybrid)?
questions.answer: It is still a set model, but it keeps a little local order by treating pairs of consecutive tokens as features.
questions.explanation: See 14.4.2 (p.427) and the chapter summary (p.443): bigram or trigram models consider the presence or absence of two or three consecutive tokens.
